extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, delegates, and political readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (late-18th-century American public / New York readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a proposed constitution is properly 'republican' and whether it is national, federal, or a mixture; and evaluating the convention's authority to propose such changes. Focuses on foundations, sources and operation of powers, extent of jurisdiction, amendment procedure, and legitimacy of convention action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive characters of a republic
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic is (or may be so called) 'a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential: government must be derived from the great body of society, not an inconsiderable proportion or favored class; Sufficient: persons administering it be appointed directly or indirectly by the people and hold appointments by one of the tenures specified. Examples and state constitutions are cited to illustrate these tenures and appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential vs sufficient features of republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ESSENTIAL that the government be derived from the great body of the society; it is SUFFICIENT that the persons administering it be appointed, either directly or indirectly, by the people, and that they hold their appointments by either of the tenures just specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why governments like Holland, Venice, Poland, England have been miscalled republics; uses examples from state constitutions to show how the specified tenures and modes of appointment satisfy the sufficient condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of titles of nobility and guarantee of republican form
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute prohibition of titles of nobility under the federal and State governments and the express guaranty of the republican form to each State are decisive proofs of the republican complexion of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as conclusive evidence: prohibition of nobility and guarantee to states are offered as 'the most decisive' proofs of republican character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete tests of conformity to republican standard (institutional comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare institutional features: House elected immediately by the people; Senate derives appointment indirectly from the people (through States); President indirectly derived from choice of the people; judges and other officers are the remote choice of the people; tenures (House 2 years, Senate 6 years, President 4 years, judges good behavior) conform to State examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists specific parallels with State constitutions (e.g., South Carolina, Maryland, New York, Virginia) and notes impeachment rules (President impeachable during continuance in office) and that ministerial offices' tenure will be subject to legal regulation following State examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: foundation of the constitution (federal vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine federal vs national character, examine the foundation on which it is established — whether assent/ratification is by the people as one aggregate nation or by the people as composing distinct and independent States. If ratification is 'the assent and ratification of the several States' it is a FEDERAL act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the proposed act results not from a majority of the people or majority of States, but from the assent of the several States (acting as sovereign bodies), and so is federal in foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: sources of ordinary powers (federal vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the sources from which ordinary powers are derived: if powers derive from the people (represented proportionally) it is NATIONAL; if powers derive from the States as political and coequal societies it is FEDERAL. The proposed Constitution presents both: House from the people (national), Senate from the States (federal), executive from a compound source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the compound nature of the presidential election (states in their political characters, with a compound ratio) and that the eventual election involves national representatives thrown into delegations from distinct bodies politic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: operation of powers (federal vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether the powers operate on political bodies composing the Confederacy (federal) or on individual citizens (national). If the ordinary operation is upon individual citizens, it indicates a national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that while some cases (e.g., controversies where States are parties) require viewing States in their political capacities, in ordinary and essential proceedings the government's operation on individuals marks a national character. Examples given where the Confederation already operates on individuals are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples where Confederation operates directly on individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where the old Confederation's powers operate immediately on persons and interests: captures, piracy, the post office, coins, weights and measures, trade with the Indians, claims under grants of land by different States, and courts-martial in the army and navy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that the Confederation itself is not purely federal in operation and to show that operation-on-individuals is not novel to the proposed Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: extent of powers (federal vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government implies indefinite supremacy over all persons and things that are objects of lawful government; a federal government has jurisdiction limited to certain enumerated objects and leaves residuary and inviolable sovereignty to the States. The proposed Constitution's enumeration of powers and reservation of others to the States indicate federal character in extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that because the proposed government’s jurisdiction is enumerated and the States retain residuary sovereignty, it cannot be deemed wholly national in extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: amendment authority signals (federal vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of amendment indicates character: if supreme authority resides in the majority of the people it is national; if concurrence of each State is essential it is federal. The proposed mode requires more than a majority computed by STATES (not by CITIZENS) and renders concurrence of less than the whole number of States sufficient — thus it is mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that because the plan requires computations by States and allows less than unanimous concurrence, it neither fits the pure national nor pure federal model but composes both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction for interpreting the convention's commission
rubrics_metrics.description: When construing the convention's powers, every part of the expression ought, if possible, to be allowed some meaning, and where parts cannot coincide, the less important should give way to the more important; the means should be sacrificed to the end, rather than the end to the means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies these rules to reconcile the different wordings of the Annapolis recommendation and the Congressional recommendatory act; argues that the paramount end (adequate national government and preservation of the Union) should prevail over narrower means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized scope of alterations and new provisions by the convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The commissions authorize ALTERATIONS in the body of the instrument and NEW PROVISIONS; this includes changing the title, inserting new articles, and altering old ones. Such authority need not be negated simply because parts of the old articles remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poses the burden on objectors to mark the boundary between authorized innovations and a TRANSMUTATION of government; argues substantial reform was in contemplation and therefore within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-based test for convention authority (ends over formal limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a NATIONAL and ADEQUATE government cannot be effected solely by alterations in the Confederation, the important end (establishing an adequate government and preserving the Union) justifies departing from strict adherence to the formal means described in commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that preservation of national happiness and the Union is the paramount end; therefore the convention's latitude to propose comprehensive reforms is justified even if it departs from the letter of its commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty- and necessity-based justification for informal or assumed action
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations of duty arising from the crisis itself (public exigency, overwhelming public opinion, examples of prior assumed powers) can supply defects of regular authority and justify informal and unauthorized propositions by respectable citizens or assemblies when submitted to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites past instances (committees, congresses, state conventions, assumptions by Congress) where informal or assumed action was accepted; emphasizes that submission to the people legitimizes irregular proposals and that changes of form should give way to substance in urgent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy conferred by submission to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the proposed plan is to be submitted to the people themselves, the disapprobation of that supreme authority would destroy it; conversely, their approbation would blot out antecedent errors and irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify that if the people approve a measure, earlier irregularities in how it was proposed become immaterial; thus the ultimate test of legitimacy is popular ratification.
